title: Paired t-Test for a Mean Difference
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 4.4 & 4.5 Paired t-Test for a Mean Difference
intro: Set up and carry out a one-sample t-test on paired differences, interpret the p-value, and justify a conclusion in context.

moments.title: A question about a mean
moments.text: A test compares a sample result with a hypothesized population value.

moments.title: Define the parameter
moments.text: Name the population, response variable, and any subtraction order.

moments.title: Verify conditions
moments.text: Check the design and the distribution of the appropriate observations.

moments.title: State population hypotheses
moments.text: The null states equality; choose the alternative from the question.

moments.title: A t statistic
moments.text: Measure distance from the null in estimated standard-error units.

moments.title: Calculate standard error
moments.text: Use sample variability to standardize the observed difference.

moments.title: Make a decision
moments.text: Compare the p-value with the significance level and conclude in context.

moments.title: Choose the correct tail
moments.text: The alternative determines which outcomes count as more extreme.

cards.name: Parameter
cards.text: Define the population mean before-minus-after reaction time before writing hypotheses.

cards.name: Select the method
cards.text: One-sample t-test on paired differences. Use paired differences for matched observations; use two-sample methods for independent groups.

cards.name: Conditions
cards.text: Check the actual design. For small paired samples inspect differences, not the two separate measurement distributions.

cards.name: Tail
cards.text: Choose less than, greater than, or two-sided from the investigative question before looking at the result.

cards.name: Conclusion
cards.text: Compare p with alpha, then state the strength of evidence about the population alternative in context.

questions.obj: Carry out a t hypothesis test
questions.q: The video gives 10 paired reaction times in milliseconds, with before-minus-after mean 4.9 and sample SD of differences 5.820. Test whether the mean difference is positive at 1%. Assume the pairs were randomly sampled from at least 100 eligible people, and the differences have no strong skewness or outliers.

steps.t: Define the parameter, method, and hypotheses.

work.text: Use a one-sample t-test on paired differences for the population mean before-minus-after reaction time.
The pairs are randomly sampled, the population contains at least ten times as many eligible people, and the differences are assumed free of strong skewness and outliers.

steps.t: Calculate the standard error and test statistic.
Find the p-value using the correct tail.

work.text: The alternative determines the tail; degrees of freedom come from the relevant t method.

steps.t: Compare with the significance level and conclude.

work.text: 0.012972 > 0.01; fail to reject the null hypothesis.

questions.answer: There is not convincing evidence at the 1% level that the population mean before-minus-after reaction time is greater than 0 milliseconds.

steps.title: Enter the sample information
steps.suppose: we want to test a claim about the population mean difference.
steps.observe: Enter the mean and SD of the within-person differences as one sample. Ten pairs give ten differences; do not add a second sample.
steps.expected: $t\approx2.662399$ after the null and tail are set.

steps.title: Set the null and alternative
steps.suppose: we want the p-value for the stated alternative.
do: On the test item, open [[Significance Test]].
Under [[Null hypothesis]], enter 0 in the hypothesis field.
Read the displayed t statistic, df, and p-value.
For more digits, open the three-dot output menu beside the test results.
steps.observe: Right corresponds to a positive before-minus-after mean difference.

steps.title: Make the decision
do: Write the decision and the conclusion about the population in context.
steps.observe: The significance level is used for your decision. The p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis, not as a probability that the null is true.

traps.title: Sample hypotheses
traps.weak: The null states that the observed sample mean equals a value.
traps.better: Hypotheses concern population parameters. The sample statistic supplies evidence.

traps.title: A p-value is not the probability of the null
traps.weak: The p-value is the chance the null is true.
traps.better: Assuming the null and conditions, it is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the alternative direction.

traps.title: Failure to reject proves equality
traps.weak: A large p-value proves no difference.
traps.better: It means there is insufficient evidence for the specified alternative at the chosen significance level.

traps.title: Pairing and independence
traps.weak: Two measurements on the same person are independent samples.
traps.better: Analyze within-person differences as one sample; the number of pairs is the sample size.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Use unrounded statistics to calculate the p-value. The two-sided probability is twice the appropriate one-tail area for the symmetric t distribution. A tiny p-value is not the probability of an exact observed sample.

notes.text: A before/after sequence alone cannot isolate a coffee effect from practice or time effects. A statistically significant change would not by itself establish that coffee caused it.

questions.stem: A one-sample mean test has sample mean 46, null mean 50, sample SD 8, and n=16. What is t?
why: This omits the square-root sample-size adjustment.
This is not the standardized difference.

questions.stem: A two-sided test reports p=0.03 and alpha=0.05. Which conclusion follows?
opts: Reject the null in favor of evidence of a difference
Fail to reject because p is positive
why: The result supplies evidence against equality.
A p-value conditions on the null; it does not assign its probability.

questions.stem: Twenty people are measured before and after training. What is the sample size and reference df for a paired t-test?
why: There are 20 pairs, not 40 independent units.
A one-sample t procedure on differences uses n−1.

questions.stem: An independent two-sample t-test uses which standard error?
why: Variance contributions add, and each is divided by its own sample size.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: Sixteen machines are randomly sampled from 400. Each runs a task using old and new software in randomized order. For old-minus-new task time, the differences have mean 2 seconds and SD 4 seconds, with no strong skewness or outliers.
parts: (a) Define the parameter, hypotheses, and procedure to test whether the new software is faster.
(b) Check conditions and calculate the statistic and one-sided p-value.
(c) Conclude at 5% significance and explain the role of pairing.
sample: (a) Let μd be the population mean old-minus-new time. Test H₀: μd=0 against Hₐ: μd>0 with a one-sample t-test on paired differences.
(b) The pairs are randomly selected, 16≤0.10(400), and the differences show no strong skewness or outliers. SE=4/√16=1, t=2, df=15, and p≈0.0320.
(c) Because 0.0320<0.05, reject H₀. There is convincing evidence the population mean old-minus-new time is positive. Pairing compares the same machines and accounts for dependence within each pair.
checklist: Defines the signed population mean difference.
States the correct alternative and paired method.
Calculates SE, t, df, and upper-tail p-value.
Concludes in context and explains pairing.
